segments.say: Lesson 7. Databases: sequel versus no sequel & Indexing. Relational versus document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores, acid versus B A S E, and how B-tree indexes work.

A database stores data permanently. sequel databases use tables with strict structure and transactions; no sequel databases trade some of that for flexibility and easy horizontal scale. Indexes make lookups fast. Here is an analogy. sequel is a well-organised filing cabinet with labelled folders and strict rules. no sequel is a set of flexible boxes you can keep adding anywhere. An index is the book's index at the back: jump straight to the page.

Why does this matter? "Which database and why?" appears in every design round. A few key words. Table / row / column: How sequel stores records. Primary key: Unique I D of a row. Index: Extra structure that makes lookups fast (B-tree). Transaction / acid: All-or-nothing, consistent, isolated, durable writes. no sequel: Key-value, document, wide-column or graph stores.

segments.say: How a B-tree index finds a row. Query: SELECT F R O M users W H E R E id equals 57. Without an index the D B scans every row: O of n.

segments.sec: Watch: How a B-tree index finds a row
segments.say: With a B-tree index, start at the root page: 57 is between 40 and 80.

segments.sec: Watch: How a B-tree index finds a row
segments.say: Follow the middle pointer: 57 is between 50 and 65.

segments.sec: Watch: How a B-tree index finds a row
segments.say: Reach the leaf holding 50–64 and jump straight to row 57. That's O of log n: about 3–4 page reads even for millions of rows.

segments.sec: Watch: How a B-tree index finds a row
segments.say: Leaves are linked in order, so range queries ( id BETWEEN 50 A N D 70 ) and O R D E R B Y are fast too.

segments.say: Cost: every INSERT or UPDATE must also update the index. Index what you query, not everything.

sequel (relational). Tables, schemas, joins, acid transactions (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). Great for relationships, complex queries and money: orders, payments, users. Postgres, MySQL. They scale reads with replicas; writes need sharding (Vitess, Citus) or distributed sequel (Spanner, CockroachDB).

no sequel families. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): get or put by key. Fastest. Sessions, carts, caches. Document (MongoDB): jason documents, flexible schema. Catalogs, profiles. Wide-column (Cassandra, HBase): massive write throughput, partitioned by key. Chat messages, time-series, feeds. Graph (Neo4j): relationships first. Social graphs, recommendations, dependency maps. Search (Elasticsearch): full-text search. Time-series (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB): metrics.

Indexing tips. B-tree: equality and range. Hash index: equality only. Inverted index: full-text search. Composite index (a, b) serves queries on a, or a+b, not b alone (leftmost prefix rule). Covering index contains all the queried columns, so there's no table lookup. Use EXPLAIN to see the query plan.

Say it in the interview. "I default to Postgres for transactional data with clear relationships and acid needs, indexed on the access patterns. I'd pick a wide-column store like Cassandra for huge write-heavy, key-partitioned data such as chat messages, and key-value stores for sessions and carts. The choice follows access patterns, consistency needs and scale.".

Let's compare. Schema: fixed, enforced, flexible / schema-on-read. Transactions: acid, multi-row, often single-item; B A S E / eventual. Joins: native, denormalize instead. Scaling: vertical plus replicas; sharding is hard, horizontal by design. Query: rich sequel, by key / limited. Use: payments, orders, inventory, feeds, chat, IoT, sessions, catalogs.

Pick the store. Bank transfers: Postgres / MySQL (acid). Billions of chat messages: Cassandra / HBase / DynamoDB. Session store: Redis. Product search: Elasticsearch. Friends-of-friends: Neo4j / graph D B. Metrics: time-series D B.

A likely interview question: sequel or no sequel for X? A strong answer: Start from access patterns and consistency. Relational and transactional with joins leads to sequel. Massive scale with simple key access or flexible schema leads to the right no sequel family. Many systems use both (polyglot persistence).
That's it for Databases: sequel versus no sequel & Indexing. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
